hook: The goldsmith who rediscovered perspective and raised the great dome of Florence.

pages.x: Filippo Brunelleschi was born in Florence in 1377, the son of a notary, and trained as a goldsmith. In 1401 he lost a famous contest to design bronze doors for the Baptistery to Lorenzo Ghiberti, and, legend says, gave up sculpture in disgust. With his friend Donatello he went to Rome to measure the ancient ruins.
Around 1415 he painted the Baptistery on a panel with a peephole in it. Looking through the hole at a mirror, people could not tell his picture from the real building.
pages.fx: He had worked out linear perspective, where parallel lines meet at a vanishing point. Within a few years painters were making flat walls look like windows into real space.

pages.x: The cathedral of Florence had a gap 45 metres wide where a dome should go, and no one knew how to build one. Brunelleschi refused to show his plans, but challenged his rivals to stand an egg on its end. None could. He cracked its bottom on the table and stood it up. "We could have done that," they said. "Yes, and you would say the same if you saw my plans."

From 1420 to 1436 he built the dome without the forest of wooden supports everyone thought it would need, using two shells, one inside the other, and bricks laid in a herringbone pattern. He invented ox-driven hoists to lift the materials. It is still the largest brick dome ever built.
In 1421 Florence granted him what is often called the first modern patent, for a giant boat to carry marble up the river Arno. On its first trip it sank, with all its marble.

Brunelleschi was the first great architect of the Renaissance. His dome still crowns Florence, his perspective changed how artists painted, and his clean, classical churches set a style for centuries.
pts: Built the dome of Florence Cathedral
